0.rationale: In chapters 1–2, Sharp appears as a named public supporter and legal advocate who independently intervenes in a complex social cause, roles that fit an established adult rather than a youth.

1.rationale: In chapter 2, his steady, serious, and sustained commitment to abolitionist work suggests the same mature adult life stage, with no textual cue of a younger developmental position.

2.rationale: In chapter 3, being publicly praised as an approved friend and benefactor reflects a settled, socially recognized humanitarian identity characteristic of an established adult.

probes.scenario: At Sharp's lodgings, a frightened Black sailor is shown in by a mutual acquaintance, carrying a torn paper and saying a merchant means to seize him before nightfall as runaway property. The acquaintance asks whether Sharp will take the matter in hand, while two other reform-minded visitors in the room wait upon his word.
probes.question: How does Granville Sharp respond when the man's plea becomes the concern of everyone present?

phase_responses.gt_action: Sharp takes the paper, questions the sailor closely, and bids the acquaintance bring the merchant's name and address.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Be composed, my friend; if there be wrong here, we must search it out by law.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He reads the case first as a particular injury requiring his own exertion. The others' presence heartens him, yet his mind fixes on facts, names, and the nearest lawful means of rescue.

voice.note: This fits Sharp's early presentation as a calm, legally minded, independently acting abolitionist ally, with era-appropriate diction and no knowledge beyond the opening chapters.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on a specific case as a particular wrong demanding Sharp's own immediate legal intervention, which is most characteristic of the initial independently intervening advocate phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: Sharp examines the paper and asks one visitor to note the particulars for friends already engaged in such causes.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let us have the truth plainly, and then we shall know how best to support you.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He sees not an isolated distress only, but another instance of a standing evil that faithful friends must steadily answer. His part is still active, though he now leans more naturally into known allies and continued support.

voice.note: The response fits Sharp's steady, serious abolitionist manner at chapter 2, using period-plausible language and appropriately showing him as an active helper who now works through trusted allies rather than as a newly celebrated public benefactor.

phase_fit.note: The thought emphasizes steady, ongoing response to a recurring evil through trusted allies and continued support, which fits sustained reformist steadiness more than either initial case-specific intervention or explicit public praise as a benefactor.

phase_responses.gt_action: Sharp reads the paper aloud to the room and invites the company to join in securing counsel and witness for the sailor.
phase_responses.gt_speech: This poor man must not stand alone; I trust we shall be found ready in his defence.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He construes the appeal as a call to the whole humane circle, not merely to his private conscience. Public trust laid upon him makes him feel bound to gather others openly into the work of protection.

voice.note: The action, speech, and thought fit Sharp’s chapter-3 phase as a grave, publicly trusted abolitionist benefactor, and the diction remains suitably eighteenth-century and communal rather than anachronistic or overly modern.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on public trust and openly gathering a humane circle into collective protection, which fits Sharp as a publicly recognized benefactor within an abolitionist community more than as a merely independent case advocate.

world.note: The scenario fits the late-18th-century Equiano world with plausible abolitionist-era actors and no anachronism or magic, and while it echoes Sharp’s known role as a legal helper to endangered Black sailors, it does not directly reproduce a specific canonical scene from chapter 1.

weak_pairs.note: Both phases still show Sharp actively taking charge of the case, with Phase 1 only mildly broadening his framing from personal intervention to support through existing abolitionist allies.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 is separated because the response shifts clearly toward public, collective handling of the plea, with Sharp explicitly gathering the room into a recognized humane circle rather than primarily acting as the individual case advocate.

probes.scenario: At the village market, a bound farmhand begs Granville Sharp for help, saying a wealthy landholder means to carry him away despite his claim of free birth. Neighbors gather in a tight ring, waiting to see whether Granville will speak into the quarrel.
probes.question: How does Granville Sharp respond as the crowd watches and the farmhand looks to him?

phase_responses.gt_action: Granville steps beside the farmhand and demands the landholder name his right before the gathered villagers.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If you claim this man, show by what right you hold him.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Granville reads the moment as a plain wrong that must be checked by a man willing to stand forward. If no one speaks now, the poor fellow may be lost before justice can be sought.

voice.note: The action, speech, and thought fit Sharp's early-phase role as a principled adult legal advocate who publicly intervenes against an apparent injustice, and the diction is suitably plain and era-appropriate.

phase_fit.note: The response centers on Sharp's own immediate intervention in a specific injustice—publicly challenging the claimant because someone must act now—rather than on communal recognition or praise within an abolitionist circle.

phase_responses.gt_action: Granville places himself near the farmhand and calls on the reeve and elders to hear the claim in open market.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let this be heard before honest men, not settled by force.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Granville still sees a duty to protect the vulnerable, but he leans on known village judgment rather than his own solitary stand. What matters is keeping the matter within a trustworthy moral circle.

voice.note: The response fits Sharp’s steady, serious reformist temper at this phase, and its appeal to open hearing and communal judgment suits both the pre-industrial setting and his slight tilt from solitary intervention toward trusted moral support.

phase_fit.note: The thought emphasizes ongoing duty filtered through trusted communal judgment rather than solitary intervention or explicit public praise, which best fits sustained reformist steadiness.

phase_responses.gt_action: Granville stands with the farmhand and invites the gathered neighbors to witness and uphold the man's claim together.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You all know me; stand with me now, and let no free man be taken quietly.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Granville understands the crowd itself as part of the remedy: their trust can shield the oppressed as much as his voice can. He feels his place as a recognized friend of the vulnerable, answerable before others as well as for them.

voice.note: The appeal to public witness and shared duty fits Sharp's phase as a publicly affirmed benefactor, and the diction is broadly period-appropriate and morally earnest, though slightly generalized.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on Sharp's recognized public role and the crowd's trust as a communal protective force, which best matches the publicly affirmed benefactor phase rather than merely independent intervention or steady support.

world.note: The market dispute fits a pre-industrial agrarian setting with no source-world leakage or obvious anachronisms, Granville Sharp remains the named protagonist throughout, and all three phase summaries present him consistently as an adult in the required life stage.

weak_pairs.note: Both phases still show Sharp actively intervening for the threatened man, with only a mild shift in thought and speech from solitary challenge toward trusted communal procedure rather than a strongly different stance on the advocate-vs-circle axis.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 is separated because the response moves from relying on fair communal hearing to explicitly invoking Sharp's recognized public standing and the crowd's shared abolitionist witness.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
I hope to have the satisfaction of seeing the renovation of liberty
and justice resting on the British government, to vindicate the honour
of our common nature. These are concerns which do not perhaps belong
to any particular office: but, to speak more seriously to every man of
sentiment, actions like these are the just and sure foundation of
future fame; a reversion, though remote, is coveted by some noble
minds as a substantial good. It is upon these grounds that I hope and
expect the attention of gentlemen in power. These are designs
consonant to the elevation of their rank, and the dignity of their
stations: they are ends suitable to the nature of a free and generous
government; and, connected with views of empire and dominion, suited
to the benevolence and solid merit of the legislature. It is a pursuit
of substantial greatness.--May the time come--at least the speculation
to me is pleasing--when the sable people shall gratefully commemorate
the auspicious æra of extensive freedom. Then shall those persons[Z]
particularly be named with praise and honour, who generously proposed
and stood forth in the cause of humanity, liberty, and good policy;
and brought to the ear of the legislature designs worthy of royal
patronage and adoption. May Heaven make the British senators the
dispersers of light, liberty, and science, to the uttermost parts of
the earth: then will be glory to God on the highest, on earth peace,
and goodwill to men:--Glory, honour, peace, &c. to every soul of man
that worketh good, to the Britons first, (because to them the Gospel
is preached) and also to the nations. 'Those that honour their Maker
have mercy on the poor.' 'It is righteousness exalteth a nation; but
sin is a reproach to any people; destruction shall be to the workers
of iniquity, and the wicked shall fall by their own wickedness.' May
the blessings of the Lord be upon the heads of all those who
commiserated the cases of the oppressed negroes, and the fear of God
prolong their days; and may their expectations be filled with
gladness! 'The liberal devise liberal things, and by liberal things
shall stand,' Isaiah xxxii. 8. They can say with pious Job, 'Did not I
weep for him that was in trouble? was not my soul grieved for the
poor?' Job xxx. 25.

As the inhuman traffic of slavery is to be taken into the
consideration of the British legislature, I doubt not, if a system of
commerce was established in Africa, the demand for manufactures would
most rapidly augment, as the native inhabitants will insensibly adopt
the British fashions, manners, customs, &c. In proportion to the
civilization, so will be the consumption of British manufactures.

The wear and tear of a continent, nearly twice as large as Europe, and
rich in vegetable and mineral productions, is much easier conceived
than calculated.

A case in point.--It cost the Aborigines of Britain little or nothing
in clothing, &c. The difference between their forefathers and the
present generation, in point of consumption, is literally infinite.
The supposition is most obvious. It will be equally immense in
Africa--The same cause, viz. civilization, will ever have the same
effect.

anchor.note: The scenario fits the passage’s public, legislative appeal, the quoted speech is verbatim and the action accurately paraphrases his blessings and exhortation toward liberty and commerce in Africa, while the thought is a reasonable inference from the passage’s emphasis on public moral witness, national righteousness, and future praise for humane advocates.
